<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values across all 20 models (ranging from -23.92 to -23.38). This indicates that a single standard condition is insufficient to break parameter degeneracy, as most models have enough flexibility to fit a simple progress curve.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but the models remain clustered. The goal for this turn is to introduce strong perturbations to separate models based on their structural differences (e.g., product/substrate inhibition or non-linear catalyst dependence).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To effectively differentiate the models, we need to test their responses to product and substrate extremes simultaneously. By introducing the maximum allowed initial product concentration (P=0.5), we can strongly isolate models that feature product-induced deactivation or product inhibition (M5, M12, M17). Models lacking these features will struggle to fit the delayed or altered kinetics. Simultaneously, using the maximum substrate concentration (S=5.0) will amplify any substrate-dependent deactivation or higher-order substrate binding (M7, M11, M16). Finally, reducing the catalyst concentration to 0.05 (compared to 0.1 in the first run) provides leverage to detect non-linear catalyst dependencies, such as dimerization (M2, M3) or bimolecular deactivation (M13, M18, M19). This multi-axis perturbation will force models with different mechanistic assumptions to diverge significantly in their global fits across the two runs.
</hypothesis>
